item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers have a 100-win season. With a victory over the Philadelphia Phillies on Thursday night, the 2026 Brew Crew improved to 100-59 on the 2026 season, reaching an unbelievable milestone that hadn't been accomplished in the first 57 seasons of the franchise's history.
After projection models expected the Brewers to finish with somewhere between 80-85 wins during the 2026 season, Pat Murphy's squad has proved the preseason predictions wrong once again. However, they didn't just surpass their expected win total by a few games; they blew past the projections, produced the best regular season in franchise history, and reached the elusive 100-win mark.
It's an unbelievable accomplishment, one that is made even more impressive by the fact that Milwaukee has produced 90+ win seasons in each of the last four seasons and five times in the last six years. This isn't a one-off season in which the Brewers sacrificed their future and went "all in" on one year. Rather, it's just another chapter in what has easily been the most successful stretch of seasons in franchise history. Put another way, to win 100 games with the best farm system in baseball makes the achievement that much more incredible.
It took a pair of wins over the Philadelphia Phillies, who still have plenty to play for, to achieve 100 wins before their final series of the regular season. With the Brewers fully in postseason preparation mode, made clear by a number of roster and in-game decisions, Murphy's team displayed their impressive depth in their late-September series victory over the Phillies. Said roster depth will be key in the postseason.
Brewers' rely on impressive roster depth to reach elusive 100-win mark after postseason preparation has begun
The Brewers entered Thursday night's series finale against the Phillies with a first-round bye, and therefore a spot in the NLDS, already secured. They didn't have nearly as much to play for as Philadelphia, who is fighting to secure home-field advantage in the Wild Card Series. As a result, Murphy turned to Shane Drohan, who is expected to be a reliever in October, for a short start, didn't include Christian Yelich or Jackson Chourio in the starting lineup, and opted to have William Contreras DH during the series finale on Thursday night. Murphy didn't use Abner Uribe or Trevor Megill and kept Antonio Senzatela in for a save in the ninth inning, and yet, even with their postseason preparation fully underway, the Brewers knocked off the mighty Phillies, who have not officially clinched a spot in the postseason just yet.
In other words, the Brewers won their 100th game of the season on Thursday night due to their impressive roster depth. Murphy's squad proved that they can defeat a postseason team like the Phillies without using one of their top starters, without starting Chourio or Yelich, and without turning to their elite high-leverage duo at the end of the ballgame.
That type of roster depth bodes well for Milwaukee's chances in October. A deep postseason run, like the one the Brewers are hoping to put together, requires contributions throughout the roster. Whether it be a pinch-hit appearance, escaping a jam in the middle innings, or serving as a defensive replacement late in the game, the 26 Brewers that Milwaukee elects to include on their postseason roster will each have their role. It's therefore encouraging to see so many of them contribute to the Brewers' late-season series win over the Phillies, which led to 100 wins.
The Brewers have three games left to improve their record-breaking regular season record even further. Expect a similar strategy, in which Murphy relies on his depth to give necessary rest to each of his players, in the Brewers' upcoming weekend series against the St. Louis Cardinals. That said, regardless of how the final series plays out, the 2026 Brewers officially have a 100-win season to their name -- a truly incredible accomplishment.

item.content:encoded:
Brewers take down Phillies for franchise's first 100-win season
(Photo credit: Bill Streicher)
Jake Bauers' RBI single in the eighth inning plated the go-ahead run Thursday for the Milwaukee Brewers, who reached the 100-win mark for the first time in franchise history with their 5-1 win over the hosting Philadelphia Phillies.
Bauers, who went 2-for-5 and added a double, singled up the middle, allowing Jackson Chourio to score from second, giving the Brewers (100-59) a 2-1 lead and starting a three-run frame. Chourio, who pinch-hit for designated hitter William Contreras, led off the frame with a walk off Jose Alvarado (5-4) and stole second.
Gary Sanchez singled deep to left field to put runners on the corners, and after Alvarado got Luis Lara to line out to shallow center, Cooper Pratt (2-for-3) welcomed Chase Shugart with another hit up the middle to give the Brewers a two-run lead. Joey Ortiz added a two-out hit, a blooper to shallow center that allowed Sanchez to score from second.
Chourio added a solo home run, his 25th blast of the season, in the ninth.
Five Brewers pitchers held the Phillies (87-72) to just four hits. JoJo Romero (3-3) allowed one hit in 1 1/3 innings against St. Louis, who Milwaukee acquired him from last month. Romero picked up his second win with the Brewers since coming off the injured list (appendectomy) earlier this month.
Antonio Senzatela relieved Romero, allowing a walk over the final 1 2/3 innings to earn his fourth save.
Phillies starter Andrew Painter held the Brewers to just one run over six innings. The rookie allowed five hits and three walks while matching a season-high eight strikeouts. His only blemish came in the second, when Sal Frelick doubled home Sanchez.
Kyle Schwarber (2-for-4) and Bryce Harper (2-for-4) combined to get all four of the Phillies hits. Harper's third-inning single scored Schwarber, who led off the frame with a double off Brewers starter Shane Drohan. Philadelphia managed just one hit, a Schwarber single in the seventh, against the Brewers bullpen.
Besides losing the game, the Phillies may also have lost infielder Luis Arraez, who reportedly sprained an ankle trying to avoid a tag on a groundout in the sixth inning.
With the win, Milwaukee can officially clinch home-field advantage throughout the postseason should the Los Angeles Dodgers lose Thursday night to the visiting San Diego Padres.
Philadelphia remains in an NL wild-card spot, but the Phillies could not drop their magic number to clinch from two.
--Field Level Media

Inside Miz's Rise: How Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski Became MLB’s Most Unhittable Starter
This week, Brewers flamethrower and National League Cy Young favorite Jacob Misiorowski will conclude one of the most overpowering, unhittable seasons ever recorded by a starting pitcher.
No qualified starter in modern baseball history has ever surrendered a lower opponent’s batting average than what Misiorowski is allowing now (.159). Take away the shortened 2020 season, and only one starter — Gerrit Cole in 2019 — has ever generated a higher strikeout rate over the course of a full season than Misiorowski’s 38.2% mark this year.
So, it might seem strange that MLB’s velocity king — whose triple-digit heat has reached as high as 105.5 mph, the fastest ever recorded by a starting pitcher — grew up idolizing a pitcher whose average career four-seam velocity clocked in around 90 mph.
Adam Wainwright, who can count on one hand how many big leaguers have ever told him he was one of their favorite players, was taken aback when I told him that he was Misiorowski’s childhood idol.
"He might’ve gotten the first 92, 93 mph from me," Wainwright quipped. "The other 12 are on him."
As of a month ago, Misiorowski had never met or talked to Wainwright. But as a kid in the Kansas City area with little winning baseball to watch in the early 2000s, Misiorowski was drawn to the St. Louis right-hander — not because Wainwright overwhelmed his competition with sheer force, the way Misiorowski can do, but because he was unflappable.
"The biggest thing was his demeanor on the mound," Misiorowski told me last month. "Something bad happens, move onto the next pitch. There’s no care, no emotion with it. I took that into just pitching in general. Whenever I give up a home run or something like that, ‘OK, so be it, they got to me, next pitch.’"
That, admittedly, was not always so easy for Misiorowski.
(Getty Images)
"They used to tear me up, and I’d get really upset on the mound," Misiorowski said. "Then I started watching other guys. I kind of thought about Wainwright and his demeanor and just everyone in the past and kind of was like, ‘That’s what I need to do. I need to forget about it.’"
Along with harnessing his control, adding to his powerful arsenal and maturing into his 6-foot-7-inch frame, Misiorowski’s mental growth on the mound is part of the transformation that has helped the raw prospect with elite tools develop into MLB’s most dominant starter over the course of just one year.
The best pitcher on the best team in baseball leads MLB in ERA, WHIP, strikeouts, strikeout rate and opponents’ batting average, among a litany of categories.
"Emotionally, he’s in a way better place," Brewers manager Pat Murphy told me. "I always say, your first year you’re on rollerskates. You don’t feel the concrete on the ground. It’s a little slippery. I feel like he’s taken off the rollerskates. He’s not all the way there. He’s not all the way matured. He’s going to face more adversity. But he’s handled what adversity has come his way pretty darn well."
‘Unlike Anything You Ever See’
Despite his junior college background, Misiorowski’s stuff was never a question.
The velocity that "Miz" generated from his long levers was enough to convince the Brewers to spend a second-round pick in 2022 on the gangly right-hander from Crowder College, who would otherwise have been transferring to LSU for his junior season.
(Photo by Tim Nwachukwu/Getty Images)
In his first full pro season in Milwaukee’s system in 2023, Misiorowski jumped from Low-A to High-A to Double-A, combining to strike out 110 batters in 71.1 innings. Days before Misiorowski’s first Double-A start against the Montgomery Biscuits, his pitching coach, Will Schierholz, saw him throw in person for the first time. The first pitch of the bullpen session clocked in at 98 mph. Then Misiorowski spun a slider at 92.
"We had some pretty good arms, some major league arms, on that staff, and you’re awestruck when you watch Miz throw up close for the first time," Schierholz, who’s now a Brewers assistant pitching coordinator, told me. "It’s unlike anything you ever see."
In Misiorowski’s last three starts that season, he struck out 29 batters in just 14.2 innings. He’d spike curveballs into the dirt, and opponents would still chase. He’d fire fastballs three feet above the zone, and hitters would still helplessly offer. Many times, they were simply guessing as soon as the ball left his hand.
"Every time he touched the mound, he knew hitters did not have a chance," Schierholz said. "If he made his pitch, they didn’t have a chance."
The problem, however, was that Misiorowski often didn’t know where the ball was going. In five starts at Double-A that season, Misiorowski walked 16 batters and hit 11.
"He was always ultra, ultra competitive, it just wasn’t always a consistent mindset on the mound when things maybe didn’t go his way," Schierholz recalled. "So to see kind of where that’s gone over the last couple years here, to see him have that consistent mindset, calm and collected at all times, that’s come a long way since he came up to Biloxi in 2023."
(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)
As the strikeouts continued to rack up a year later, so did the free passes. Over 79.2 innings at Double-A in 2024, Misiorowski struck out 105 batters, walked 50 and plunked 10.
When he was promoted to Triple-A that August, the Brewers put him in the bullpen, in part to limit his innings. He clearly had a big-league arm, but his lack of control threatened to make him a reliever long-term.
"I think that was always in the back of everybody’s head, right?" Schierholz said. "Especially for a guy with that prolific stuff. Just in general, you don’t see starters have the stuff that he has. But I think the thing that always kept all of us optimistic is the arsenal’s deep. He didn’t have a big injury history, and he was still so young that we had time to make sure this played out in a positive way."
(Photo by Olivia Vega/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Misiorowski returned to starting at the beginning of the 2025 season at Triple-A. The control issues lingered, which was part of the reason he was MLB’s No. 68 overall prospect that year and not a top-10 talent. Over a five-start stretch, he struck out 38 batters in 30.2 innings with a 0.79 ERA. But then came four starts in which he combined for 12 walks over 14 innings.
Still, despite Misiorowski’s volatility, depth issues in the Brewers’ big-league rotation spurred action. They called up the 23-year-old, who did not look overwhelmed by the promotion.
After just five MLB starts, the last of which was a six-inning, 12-strikeout gem against Clayton Kershaw and the reigning champion Dodgers, Misiorowski was named an All-Star. Some scoffed at MLB’s decision, but he looked deserving of the honor when he threw a scoreless eighth inning in an eventual National League win.
"He’s taken the game straight out of the firehose," Brewers pitching coach Chris Hook told me. "It was a lot. I thought he did an incredible job for as much as was thrown at him."
But adversity beckoned, as it does so often for rookies.
An Early Turning Point
Opponents went from hitting .138 against Misiorowski in the first half to .257 in the second half. Lefties feasted on his slider, his strikeout rate declined, his control and command remained spotty, and the Brewers wanted to be cautious of his workload, considering he had never thrown even 100 innings in a professional season.
Hook sensed Misiorowski was wearing down, both physically and mentally.
"The intensity here is higher, and then you’re pitching more often," Hook explained. "At the end of September, he felt it. It was a lot of strain."
(Photo by Olivia Vega/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
After Misiorowski registered a 5.45 ERA in nine starts out of the break, he was moved to the bullpen at the end of the season. He didn’t like the way he was handling himself or how he handled getting hit around.
So, he thought back to Wainwright. About the mindset. About letting go.
Then, he rose to the occasion with the lights at their brightest.
In a bulk relief role, Misiorowski recorded a 1.50 ERA over 12 playoff innings. His postseason ended with five innings of one-run ball at Dodger Stadium, where he struck out nine batters in Game 3 of the National League Championship Series. It wasn’t enough to lift his Brewers over the eventual back-to-back champs, but he looked at that moment as a turning point in his career.
"I went through the struggles at the end of the year, and really was trying to battle through it," Misiorowski said. "Then, postseason rolled around, had the success, and I kind of brought it into this year, still on that momentum."
He demonstrated his ability to control his emotions on baseball’s biggest stage.
Then he focused on everything else within his control — his body, his arsenal, the strike zone — to ascend into a starting pitching marvel.
"When you fail, and you’ve been one of the best pitchers on the planet and quickly one of the youngest All-Stars of all time, I’m sure that can take a toll on anybody," Brewers president of baseball operations Matt Arnold told me. "But he’s a mature kid. He’s grown up to be a man right in front of us, and he’s a guy that you want at the front of any rotation. He’s the best pitcher in the game, in my opinion."
Controlling His Body
Over the offseason, Misiorowski went to work on building his slender frame, knowing he needed more force and stamina to hold up over the long haul of a season after last year’s dropoff.
"It was definitely more lower-body focused," he told me. "I wanted to get my legs as strong as possible. That’s where most of my power comes from."
He ended last year around 185 pounds. Crossing the 200-pound mark this winter was a milestone moment. He didn’t stop. He said he came into camp at around 215-220 pounds and is now around 210-215, a 30-pound increase from last year.
He didn’t change his diet entirely, but he acknowledged there were fewer 3 a.m. visits to Taco Bell with his friends.
"Eating well, eating better," Misiorowski explained, "not crappy, like I was. Really working on finally maturing into my body."
Where does he see the weight helping most now?
"The biggest is definitely stamina," he said. "The effort isn’t max effort every time. You can still get to the 100s, and it’s an easier effort compared to last year when I was hitting 100 and it was full go."
Of all the improvements Misiorowski has made, it’s the velocity jump that stands out most to Schierholz, his old minor-league pitching coach. What Misiorowski is doing is unmatched and unprecedented.
(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)
Prior to this season, the fastest average four-seamer for a qualified MLB starter over the course of a full season belonged to Noah Syndergaard at 98.9 mph in 2016. Misiorowski is averaging 100.6 mph this year, up more than a tick from a season ago.
There have been 365 occasions of a starting pitcher crossing the 102-mph mark this season. The Pirates’ Bubba Chandler did it twice. So did Dodgers reliever Edgardo Henriquez, when he was used as an opener. The other 361 times are courtesy of Misiorowski, who has also eclipsed 103 mph 143 times, 104 mph 22 times and 105 mph once.
A year ago, he threw just 22 pitches over 102 mph, including the postseason.
"I think we try to lay out plans for the guys, but all the credit goes to him, the work that he put in," Arnold said. "You gotta want to be great, and I think Miz is exactly that kind of kid. He knew what he needed to do to get better, and he did it himself."
And now, Misiorowski has a better idea of where his four-seamer is going — even if he’s not entirely sure why.
Controlling The Zone
Misiorowski’s fastball gets the highlights and acclaim, but arguably the most dramatic and important change Misiorowski made this year has nothing to do with his power.
He has cut his walk rate down from 11% last year to 6.6% this year, the largest year-to-year drop among all qualified MLB starters.
But he can’t explain how.
(Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images)
"I honestly have no clue," Misiorowski told me. "I wish I could tell you and help everyone out. I honestly have zero idea on how I’m doing it. It’s one of those things I’m looking at like, ‘That number ain’t right.’"
Many of his teammates assumed he must be pounding the strike zone a lot more, but he’s actually in the zone less this year than he was last season.
That might seem confusing, but his pitching coach has an explanation.
"You can’t wait him out," Hook said. "He’s throwing 105 [mph], and it’s like, ‘I gotta go if he’s throwing a strike.’"
"It’s going to be hard to put the ball in play," Arnold added, "so teams are probably wanting to be aggressive and see if they can hop on something."
It helps that Misiorowski is throwing a first-pitch strike 8% more this year than last year — also the largest year-to-year jump from any qualified starter this season.
And it plays into Brewers closer Trevor Megill’s theory.
"You make one pitch a strike on the corner, then the one off the corner by three inches looks like it’s closer than it is," Megill told me.
Misiorowski’s chase rate (35.2%) is up nearly 7% from last season.
Meanwhile, his whiff rate (37.2%) is the highest among all qualified starters and is also up significantly from a year ago (29.7%) — again, that’s the biggest year-to-year jump for a starting pitcher in MLB.
Misiorowski’s enhanced ability to harness his stuff has led to shorter innings, longer outings and even a game between him and his pitching coach.
One time earlier this year, Misiorowski was coming off a 12-pitch frame when Hook issued a test.
"I said, ‘Hey, can you make it a 10 next?’ He made it a 10,’" Hook recalled. "I said, ‘Can you make it a nine?’ We just like having those challenges inside the game."
Controlling His Arsenal
Earlier this year, Cardinals shortstop Masyn Winn watched Misiorowski’s fastball up close and followed up with a question.
Why the hell are you throwing anything else?
"It was funny," Misiorowski recalled. "But on the flipside, I’m like, ‘I can’t just do that.’"
In some ways, though, Misiorowski has heeded Wynn’s advice.
His four-seam usage is up this year, and no starter in baseball throws their heater more. With a fastball that averages over 100 mph and is responsible for 163 of his MLB-leading 247 strikeouts, you can understand why.
At the same time, Misiorowski is still adding to his repertoire.
"It seems to me like he went home and said, ‘You know what, the postseason was fun, I want to get back there again, how can I be a great pitcher and not just a thrower?’" Wainwright said. "That is the nature of how great players mature. That’s the nature of how great players grow in the game. They don’t get comfortable in who they are. They don’t get stuck."
Last year, lefties hit .385 and righties hit .267 against Misiorowski’s slider, which averaged 5 mph slower than his four-seamer. The Brewers wanted to find another offering that would create more of a separation in velocity.
So, Misiorowski added a slower slider with more depth to his arsenal this year, which righties are hitting .188 against. Meanwhile, he turned last year’s slider into his cutter, which lefties are hitting .089 against this season.
"I’ve gotten a lot of strange looks, strange emotions, from it, just in the fact that the cutter’s kind of closer to the heater," Misiorowski said. "You get some swings where some guys see the spin, and then they’re like, ‘Oh, shoot, it’s on me.’"
(Photo by Larry Radloff/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)
In addition to his curveball and changeup, the new additions to his arsenal give opponents more to think about this season beyond his velocity.
"He kind of does things on the fly a little bit," Hook said. "I’m not saying he’s a lab kid, per se. He’s naturally gifted, and he’s like, ‘I’m going to do this,’ ‘I can do that,’ and he makes the adjustment."
Along with a lower walk rate, Misiorowski’s strikeout rate is up 6.2% from last season and is the highest in MLB. He won’t win the triple crown — Phillies ace Cristopher Sánchez has three more wins than him — but he leads the sport in both ERA and strikeouts, despite ranking 23rd in innings pitched.
His triple-digit heat combined with better control and command certainly help, but so does the tweak in his repertoire. He’s also gaining a better feel for game-planning and why his catchers are calling for certain pitches in certain situations.
"At the start of the year, we were definitely more, ‘Whatever you think, let’s just roll with it. You’re obviously seeing something that’s working,’" Misiorowski told me. "And it’s gotten to the point where it’s like, ‘OK, I’m kinda seeing it too. I understand where you’re going with this."
‘This Guy Is Built For This’
More often than not, though, he relies on his catchers to help him navigate a game, as William Contreras did during his 15-strikeout, one-hit, complete-game shutout on 95 pitches against the Phillies in June.
Contreras also helped Misiorowski work around trouble two months later, when the pitcher made his return to the mound at Dodger Stadium for the first time since the NLCS.
(Photo by Michael Reaves/Getty Images)
A year ago, Misiorowski was stupefied watching Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman sign his jersey at the All-Star Game. In some ways, he’s still that wide-eyed kid, pinching himself about his new reality.
"I don’t think that will ever get to a point where it’s just normal," Misiorowski told me.
Only now, he’s starting to gain the poise of the idols he grew up watching.
The day before his start on Aug. 15, Misiorowski’s newfound confidence was on full display when he gave away his attack plan against Ohtani.
"He knows what I’m going to do: I’m going to throw a heater," Misiorowski vowed. "Good luck. Here it is."
Sure enough, he followed up on those words by attacking Ohtani with six straight fastballs in his first at-bat, all over 102 mph, to induce a popout. But it’s what Misiorowski did in his final at-bat against Ohtani that exemplified why he is so much more than the novice flamethrower he was a year ago.
After three straight singles off Misiorowski in the fifth inning, Ohtani stepped to the plate with the bases loaded and one out. This time, at Contreras’ behest, Misiorowski switched it up. He got a swinging strike on a curveball, a called strike on a four-seamer, then sent Ohtani back to the dugout swinging through a slider.
"He’s thinking more like a pitcher," Contreras told me, "and not just wanting to throw hard."
(Photo by Keith Birmingham/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News via Getty Images)
One batter later, Misiorowski used the slider again to fool Freddie Freeman on a strikeout and escape the threat. He pumped his fist and let out a scream before returning to the dugout.
As he attempts to follow Wainwright’s lead with his composure on the mound, he’s not losing himself in the process.
"That part of his game hasn’t changed, which I’m happy to see," Schierholz said. "That’s part of what makes him special, is the competitiveness and pitching with emotion, as long as he continues to rein it in and keep it in control."
The Brewers are counting on that as they rumble toward the best record in baseball for a second straight season, this time hoping their Cy Young favorite can help them author a new ending to their franchise’s winningest chapter.
"Obviously, it’s a different animal when you get into October," Misiorowski said. "But it’s going to be exciting, and I think we have a team that can make a run at it."
"This guy," Hook added, "is built for this."

item.title: [Bozeman Daily Chronicle] Yelich, Turang homer as Brewers win 99th game of season, delay Phillies' possible playoff clinch

item.content:encoded:
PHILADELPHIA (AP) — Christian Yelich and Brice Turang hit solo home runs, and the Milwaukee Brewers delayed Philadelphia’s potential postseason clinch with a 4-1 win over the Phillies on Wednesday night.
The Phillies needed both a win over the Brewers and a loss later Wednesday night by either Arizona or San Diego to secure their fifth straight trip to the National League playoffs. The Phillies started their run with a trip to the World Series in 2022, reached the NL Championship Series the next season and are coming off consecutive NL East titles.
The Phillies have to settle for a wild-card berth this season and are likely to open the playoffs next week on the road. The Phillies, Chicago and San Diego hold the three NL wild cards headed into the final games of the season.
The Phillies went 0 for 12 with runners in scoring position against the Brewers and left 10 runners on base.
Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly said ahead of the game the team was willing to wait at Citizens Bank Park until after the Padres game ended, if necessary, to celebrate. No need to hang around.
Aaron Nola (7-11) had turned around a miserable season and posted a 1.86 ERA over his last eight starts as the longest-tenured Phillie got the chance to clinch. With a playoff party looming, he instead surrendered Turang’s 20th homer of the season in the first inning and Yelich’s 12th of the year in the second.
The Phillies scored their only run in the second inning after loading the bases with no outs against Brewers starter Logan Henderson (11-3). Henderson allowed four hits and one run over five innings to help the NL Central champion Brewers win their 99th game of the season.
Trevor Megill worked a scoreless ninth for his 30th save.
William Contreras extended his hitting streak to 11 games with a two-run single in the third for a 4-1 lead.
Nola struck out eight in six innings.
Up next
The Brewers did not announce a starter for Thursday's game. The Phillies send RHP Andrew Painter (3-10, 5.59 ERA) to the mound.

item.title: [thereporteronline.com] Milestone strikeout a moment to reflect for Phillies’ Zack Wheeler

item.description: PHILADELPHIA — Zack Wheeler expressed, on one hand, surety Tuesday night. On the other, genuine surprise and gratitude. item.content:encoded:
PHILADELPHIA — Zack Wheeler expressed, on one hand, surety Tuesday night. On the other, genuine surprise and gratitude.
Of course, the Phillies right-handed starter went into the game against Milwaukee knowing he was on 1,997 career strikeouts. He understood what it meant that only 95 pitchers in the history of baseball – and nine active – had crossed the 2,000-strikeout threshold.
But at plenty of junctures in a big-league career that started at age 23 but got derailed for two years, he never imagined he’d reach such a round number.
“It’s really cool, special,” Wheeler said after striking out 11 Brewers in a 6-4 Phillies win. “Some of the guys asked me in here, would you ever have thought? The answer is no. Getting into the league, trying to get your feet under you, trying to last, game to game early on, just trying to stay up in the big leagues and trying to figure it out was hard for me. And just being where I am now, it’s pretty special.”
The flipside to that disbelief, though, was the rock-steady assuredness that at age 36, Wheeler could get back to where he was at 35.
On Sept. 22, 2025, Wheeler went to sleep with thoracic decompression surgery scheduled for the next day, the removal of a rib relieving a circulation issue that had led to blood clots and ended his season.
He headed home 365 days later having made his 27th and likely final start of the season, three more than last year despite a delayed start to the season. He carries a 13-5 record, a 3.06 ERA and, by wins above replacement, his third-most valuable season among seven as a Phillie.
Which has to be at least a little surprising, right?
“I would expect it,” Wheeler said when asked if he would’ve been surprised to learn these were his stats a year post-surgery. “You’ve got to have that confidence. That’s all it is. It’s just confidence. It’s not anything else than that. You have to expect to be back to who you were. You’ve got to keep that mindset. If not, then who knows what’s going to go on in your head, and that can translate to you coming back and how you perform.”
How he performed Tuesday was as he has most of the season: Rock solid. He made quick work of the milestone, striking out the side in the first inning. His 310 career games to reach 2,000 strikeouts ties Felix Hernandez for the 13th-fewest in history.
He struck out the side in the second, too. With a whiff of Luis Lara to start the third, he set the Phillies franchise record. Already in his mind was the then-major league mark he watched from the dugout in New York in 2014, when Mets teammate Jacob deGrom fanned the first eight Marlins to tie the modern record set in 1986 by Houston’s Jim Deshaies. (deGrom’s bid was broken up by a single by the pitcher, former Phillies farmhand Jarred Cosart; the MLB record was re-set in 2021 when Miami’s Pablo Lopez struck out the first nine Braves he faced.)
“All I could think about was deGrom doing that when we were down in Miami back in the day, and the pitcher came up and got the bat on the ball,” he said. “So I was just trying to beat him, honestly. Once I got through that second inning, I was like, ‘All right, I’m trying to do this.’”
Wheeler’s run was broken by a groundout to third by Cooper Pratt. He retired the first nine in order before Garrett Mitchell looped a single off the glove of a backtracking Bryson Stott at third to lead off the fourth. Mitchell scored on William Contreras’s sac fly to get the Brewers within 3-1.
A lead-off single by nine-hitter David Hamilton and a walk to Jackson Chourio put two on in the sixth. Wheeler froze Brice Turang, Hamilton and Chourio stealing third and second. Contreras beat Wheeler on a first-pitch fastball that was a little too low, the catcher golfing a liner just over the reach of a leaping Trea Turner at short for a two-run single and a 3-3 game, sending Wheeler to the no-decision.
“I wanted to go in, but it was down. I wanted it more up,” he said. “Down’s a little easier to hit than up. That’s probably what I was most upset about tonight, and probably the pitch I hate the most so far this season.”
There hasn’t been much to regret this year. Wheeler’s injury dealt a huge confidence blow to the Phillies heading into the postseason last year. It started him on the injured list in 2026, but he blew through the six month estimated timeline to debut by the end of April.
From that point on, he was the Zack Wheeler of old, so much so that he’s likely to start the first game of a Phillies Wild Card series despite not being one of the team’s two All-Star starters this season.
A month into his return, his ERA sat at 1.67, excluding a five-start stretch from late July to late August in which he allowed 23 earned runs in 24.1 innings around an rain-interrupted outing in Baltimore, he’s been spectacular, with an ERA of 2.05 over his other 22 starts.
Wheeler isn’t prone to reflection, especially midseason. The strikeout milestone forced a bit of it upon him. He still approached it as having one start left, though he’d only pitch in Sunday’s finale if the Phillies need it, which is highly avoidable at a magic number of 2 after Tuesday’s action.
He took the chance to express gratitude: to his wife and family, to the catchers and coaches he’s had through his 12 major league seasons. He reserved a special mention for Phillies head athletic trainer Paul Buchheit for the rehabilitation plan from last year.
The round number offered perspective, for a blue-chip prospect who was outstanding in his first two seasons more than a decade ago but then missed two full seasons with a complicated recovery from Tommy John surgery. He’s navigated the jump from New York to Philly for two big contracts, weathered changes to the expectations of the position, bridged eras from batting to designated hitters, from pitch clocks to ABS.
Through it all, Wheeler has continually dealt every fifth day, which is what a milestone like Tuesday’s fetes.
“The road was hard coming back from that,” Wheeler said of his Tommy John ordeal. “That was another point where I didn’t know what to expect because it was taking longer than what we all expected at the time. So, I was just trying to get back out there. It was kind of like starting over again, just trying to get back out there, just lasting, and I was able to figure it out.”

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

23 Sep 2026, 12:25 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Drew Rasmussen allowed one hit in 6 2/3 outstanding innings and the visiting Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East with a 6-1 victory over the New York Yankees on Tuesday night in the nightcap of a day-night doubleheader.
The Rays won for the 20th time in 28 games and clinched their fifth division title. Tampa Bay last won the AL East in 2021 when it won a team-record 100 games. Yandy Diaz drove in four runs on a pair of singles.
Rasmussen (16-5) took a no-hitter into the seventh until Heliot Ramos opened the inning with a double to left for New York. Ramos eventually scored on an RBI single by rookie George Lombard Jr. off Kevin Kelly.
Rasmussen finished with 11 strikeouts for his fourth career double-digit strikeout performance. He finished two shy of his career-high set June 10 against the Boston Red Sox and the Rays won his 12th consecutive start.
Yankees 2, Rays 0 (Game 1)
Cody Bellinger hit a two-run home run in the fourth inning as host New York recorded a shutout over Tampa Bay in the opener of a day-night doubleheader.
With the victory, the Yankees temporarily prevented the Rays from clinching the AL East and moved six games ahead of the Boston Red Sox for the American League's top wild-card spot.
New York's Carlos Rodon (7-3) scattered three singles over eight innings as the Yankees finished off the victory in a brisk 2 hours, 2 minutes. Rodon struck out eight in his 100th career win and also reached 1,500 strikeouts for his career. Rays right-hander Nick Martinez (15-5) allowed two runs on five hits over six innings with seven strikeouts to take his first loss since July 9.
Dodgers 7, Padres 0
Freddie Freeman drove in three runs, Will Smith and Tommy Edman hit home runs, and Los Angeles inched closer to the best record in the National League with a shutout of visiting San Diego.
Eight Dodgers pitchers held down the red-hot Padres offense in a bullpen game, with Justin Wrobleski (12-5) earning the win. Roki Sasaki struck out two in one inning in his return from a blister issue. The Dodgers extended their home winning streak to 11 games.
Los Angeles moved to within one game of the NL-best Milwaukee Brewers and reduced its magic number for a top-two NL spot and a bye into the National League Division Series to one. Luis Campusano had two hits for the Padres, whose magic number to clinch a playoff spot remained at two.
Phillies 6, Brewers 4
Bryson Stott delivered the tiebreaking hit in the eighth inning to guide Philadelphia to a victory over visiting Milwaukee. Brandon Marsh homered and knocked in three runs as the Phillies lowered their magic number to two to clinch a postseason berth.
Zack Wheeler ended up with a no-decision after striking out 11 while giving up three runs and five hits in 5 2/3 innings. Wheeler struck out the first seven batters he faced, setting a Phillies record for consecutive strikeouts to begin a game. His first-inning strikeout of Brice Turang was the 2,000th of his career.
The Brewers saw their lead over the Dodgers for the top record in the majors shrink to one as they lost just the third time in their last 13 games. William Contreras knocked in three runs.
Marlins 8, Cubs 2 (12 innings)
Griffin Conine plated the go-ahead run that ignited a six-run 12th inning for visiting Miami, which snapped a three-game losing by beating Chicago and postponing the Cubs' playoff celebration for at least a day.
On a night when runs were scarce until the final inning, both teams endured a pair of scoreless extra frames before Conine broke the drought with a leadoff, golf-shot single off Caleb Thielbar that fell just inside the left field line. Esteury Ruiz, the automatic runner, scored from second to make it 3-2 as the Marlins sent 10 batters to the plate in the inning.
The Cubs could have clinched a wild-card playoff spot with a win or Arizona loss, but neither of those happened keeping the Diamondbacks mathematically alive. Josh Ekness (3-4) struck out a pair in the 11th inning to get the win while Thielbar (3-4) gave up three runs -- two earned -- in his inning of work.
Guardians 3, Red Sox 2
Nathaniel Lowe drove in Chase DeLauter with a sacrifice fly in the ninth inning and Cleveland held on to beat host Boston in the first game of a three-game series.
Cleveland not only extended its winning streak to six but maintained its one-game lead over the Chicago White Sox for first place in the AL Central.
Parker Messick held Boston to one run on five hits in five innings, his 14th straight start allowing three runs or fewer. Payton Tolle started for the Red Sox and gave up two runs on eight hits in 5 2/3 innings as the Guardians went 1-for-12 with runners in scoring position and stranded 15.
White Sox 14, Royals 11
Chase Meidroth smacked a three-run home run among his three hits and drove in five, and Brenton Doyle, Randal Grichuk and Munetaka Murakami also homered to power Chicago past host Kansas City.
Chicago won for the fourth time in five games to remain one game behind the AL Central-leading Cleveland Guardians. The White Sox, who hold the third and final AL wild-card spot, reduced their magic number to earn a playoff berth to three.
Vinnie Pasquantino hit a ninth-inning grand slam for the Royals, who lost their fifth straight. He went 3-for-5 with a double and also drove in five.
Nationals 3, Tigers 1
CJ Abrams hit a pair of home runs and drove in all three runs as visiting Washington topped Detroit. Abrams reached 100 RBIs for the season with his solo shot in the second inning, then broke a 1-1 tie in the seventh with his 33rd long ball of the season, a two-run blast.
Dylan Crews had two hits and scored the other run for the Nationals. Rookie Jackson Kent (2-4) earned the win in long relief. He allowed one run on six hits over four innings and struck out three. Opener Riley Cornelio lasted 2 2/3 innings, striking out four and walking three.
Ben Malgeri scored the Tigers' only run. Kevin McGonigle and Max Clark each had two hits.
Pirates 2, Cardinals 0
Jared Jones and two relievers combined on a one-hitter as Pittsburgh beat visiting St. Louis for a fifth straight win. Jones (5-6) lowered his ERA to 1.08 in four September starts and struck out nine with zero walks over seven innings while throwing 63 of his 86 pitches for strikes.
Pittsburgh broke a scoreless tie with two outs in the sixth inning on Ryan O'Hearn's RBI single against Andre Pallante (12-8). Pallante allowed one run on three hits with two walks and two strikeouts over six innings.
St. Louis struck out 14 times and lost for the fifth time in its last six games.
Astros 7, Mariners 0
Christian Walker hit a three-run home run, Yordan Alvarez launched a two-run homer and Isaac Paredes added a solo shot as Houston slugged and pitched its way past host Seattle.
Jose Altuve, Yainer Diaz, Alvarez and Paredes each collected two hits for the Astros, who pulled into a first-place tie with the Texas Rangers in the West. Five Astros pitchers combined to throw a four-hit shutout. Miguel Ullola (1-0) earned his first major league win, allowing one hit and striking out two over two innings of relief.
Julio Rodriguez notched two hits for Seattle. The Mariners went 0-for-3 with runners in scoring position and stranded nine.
Reds 4, Braves 0
Brandon Williamson fired six scoreless innings and Cincinnati supported him with three solo homers to defeat host Atlanta in the opener of a three-game series.
Cincinnati ended a two-game losing streak and evened the season series with Atlanta at 2-2. Williamson (5-4) worked six scoreless innings, allowing three hits and two strikeouts. Elly De La Cruz (29), Dane Myers (8) and Eugenio Suarez (25) each hit a home run for the Reds. It was Suarez's 350th career homer, making him the 10th active player to reach that mark.
Atlanta starter JR Ritchie (1-4) pitched five innings and allowed one run on four hits and three walks. The rookie struck out a career-high eight batters.
Mets 6, Rangers 3
Francisco Alvarez laced a go-ahead two-run double in the sixth, then scored an insurance run on an unusual sacrifice fly for visiting New York, who damaged Texas' playoff hopes with a win in the opener of a three-game interleague series in Arlington.
Juan Soto had an RBI single in the third, and Carson Benge capped the scoring with a run-scoring double in the seventh for the Mets. The club won hours after removing the interim tag from manager Andy Green and signing him to a three-year extension.
Josh Jung had an RBI double in the third, and Elias Diaz and Wyatt Langford lofted sacrifice flies in the fourth for the Rangers, who entered Tuesday with a one-game lead over the Houston Astros in the AL West.
Diamondbacks 7, Rockies 2
Nolan Arenado homered and doubled among his three hits, Michael Soroka tossed seven strong innings, and Arizona kept its slim postseason hopes alive with a win over host Colorado in Denver.
Geraldo Perdomo also had three hits and Ildemaro Vargas finished with two hits for Arizona, which remains alive in the NL wild-card race, sitting four games behind Philadelphia, San Diego and the Chicago Cubs for the third and final spot with five games to go.
Mickey Moniak homered for Colorado, which finished with just three hits and just one after the third inning. The Rockies (57-100) are the first team to lose 100 or more games in four straight seasons since the 1962-65 New York Mets.
Twins 3, Giants 2
Walker Jenkins homered, Luke Keaschall contributed both offensively and defensively, and Minnesota evened its road interleague series against San Francisco.
Taj Bradley (12-6) combined with four relievers on a six-hitter for the Twins, who used two late diving catches by Keaschall in right field to prevent the Giants from taking the first two of the series.
Bradley allowed just one other hit -- a fifth-inning single by Drew Gilbert -- in his six innings. He walked three and struck out six. Keaschall's one-out triple scored Ryan Kreidler, then Brooks Lee gave Minnesota the lead for good with a run-scoring single to plate Keaschall.
A's 9, Angels 7
Carlos Cortes hit a go-ahead two-run homer in the bottom of the eighth inning and the Athletics overcame a six-run deficit to beat Los Angeles in West Sacramento, Calif.
In addition to the homer off Sam Bachman, Cortes also delivered a pinch-hit RBI triple in the seventh, helping the Athletics end a six-game losing streak. Zack Gelof hit a two-run homer later in the eighth for the A's. Shea Langeliers and Lawrence Butler each had three hits and an RBI for the Athletics.
Denzer Guzman homered and drove in four RBIs for the Angels, who have lost four of their last six games. Mike Trout added three hits and two runs for Los Angeles (60-97), which has never lost 100 games in a season.
Blue Jays at Orioles, ppd.
The scheduled game between Toronto and host Baltimore was postponed due to ongoing inclement weather. The game will be made up as part of a split doubleheader on Wednesday, with games starting at 1:35 p.m. and 6:35 p.m. ET.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
El martes por la noche, continuó dejando huella en el partido contra los Cerveceros en el Citizens Bank Park. No solo ponchó a los tres bateadores de la primera entrada, sino que también ponchó a Brice Turang para registrar el número 2,000 de su carrera.
Zack Wheeler estableció un récord para los Filis al ponchar a los primeros siete bateadores del encuentro en una victoria por 6-4 sobre los Cerveceros (98-59), superando la marca de Brandon Duckworth de seis ponches seguidos para comenzar un partido el 5 de agosto del 2002 contra los Dodgers. El ponche de Wheeler en el primer episodio ante Brice Turang fue el número 2,000 de su carrera.
Wheeler es el 96to lanzador en la historia de MLB en alcanzar los 2,000 ponches. Su compañero de equipo, Aaron Nola, llegó a esa misma cifra a principios de esta temporada. Son la segunda pareja de compañeros de equipo que alcanza dicha marca en una misma temporada, los primeros en lograrlo fueron Tim Hudson y Jake Peavy con los Gigantes en 2014.
El lanzador derecho de 36 años fue más allá al ponchar a siete bateadores consecutivos al inicio del juego, superando así el récord anterior de la franquicia de seis ponches, establecido por Brandon Duckworth en 2002.
Fue una salida fantástica contra el mejor equipo en todo el béisbol, un club al que Filadelfia podría enfrentar en la SDLN. Los Filis anotaron tres carreras en la octava entrada contra el bullpen de los Cerveceros para llevarse el triunfo.
Pero Milwaukee fabricó una carrera en el cuarto capítulo para reducir la ventaja de los Filis a 3-1. Sin embargo, en el sexto inning, un sencillo al iniciar la entrada, un boleto con un out, un doble robo y un sencillo con dos outs del venezolano William Contreras anotaron dos carreras para empatar el partido.
Jake Bauers le siguió con otro sencillo con dos outs. Fue el 101er pitcheo de la jornada para Wheeler.
Mattingly dijo antes del juego que esperaba mantener a Wheeler en cerca de 90 lanzamientos, teniendo en cuenta que podría ser su última apertura de la campaña regular. Ahora, el próximo turno de Wheeler en la rotación es el último compromiso de la temporada regular el domingo contra los Rays, pero si los Filis aseguran el Comodín de la Liga Nacional antes del domingo, podría abrir el Juego 1 de la Serie de Comodines el martes.
Los Filis quieren a Wheeler lo más fresco posible, porque si pretenden ganar esa serie al mejor de tres, casi con certeza será debido a un excelente pitcheo abridor por parte de Wheeler, el dominicano Cristopher Sánchez y otros.
La escuadra de Filadelfia (87-70) terminó el choque con la esperanza de que los Diamondbacks (82-74) cayeran ante los Rockies la noche del martes. Ganando o perdiendo, los Filis todavía podrían asegurar un quinto viaje consecutivo a la postemporada tan pronto como el miércoles.

item.content:encoded:
Zack Wheeler walked out to the mound at Citizens Bank Park Tuesday night needing three strikeouts to reach 2,000. It took him 12 pitches. Garrett Mitchell went down first. Then Jackson Chourio and Brice Turang were rung up as Wheeler reached the milestone against the Milwaukee Brewers.
But, Wheeler kept going.
William Contreras, Jake Bauers and Christian Yelich struck out in the second. Luis Lara struck out to lead off the third inning. Wheeler struck out seven straight Brewers to start the game, something no Phillies pitcher had done to start a game. Cooper Pratt finally ended it by grounding out to third.
Wheeler, 36, is the 96th pitcher in major league history to reach 2,000 strikeouts and only nine got there faster.
It came almost a year after a surgeon in St. Louis removed his top rib to address the circulation problem in his arm.
The trouble started after a start in Washington on Aug. 15, 2025. Wheeler felt some heaviness in his right shoulder. By the next morning doctors had found a blood clot near it. The diagnosis was venous thoracic outlet syndrome, meaning a vein was getting pinched between his collarbone and rib cage. The fix was taking out the first rib and some of the muscle around it. He missed the rest of the season and the playoffs.
He came back April 25 against Atlanta, capped at 90 pitches. He hasn't looked back. Wheeler entered Tuesday 13-5 with a 2.99 ERA and 177 strikeouts in 150½ innings. In his previous four starts he had allowed three runs in 26 innings.
Aaron Nola still owns the Phillies' mark for strikeouts in a row at any point in a game. He struck out 10 straight Mets in June 2021, matching Tom Seaver's major league record from 1970. The modern record for starting a game that way is nine, set by Miami's Pablo Lopez against Atlanta in 2021.
Wheeler finished with 11 strikeouts Tuesday night in 5⅔ innings.
This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Zack Wheeler opens with Phillies record 7 straight strikeouts, hits 2,000 for career

item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers are nearing the end of the MLB regular season. They defeated the Baltimore Orioles 6-5 Friday night, with Jackson Chourio driving in three runs. Prior to Game 2, the team announced news regarding Christian Yelich.
Saturday's game will feature a pitching battle between Robert Gasser and Trevor Rogers. The game will be broadcast at 3:05 PM Central Time, 4:05 PM Eastern Time. The Brewers are 8-2 in their last 10 contests, while the Orioles are 6-4.
Milwaukee Brewers Announce Big Christian Yelich News During Baltimore Orioles Series
Prior to the first pitch of their second game against the Orioles, the Brewers announced lineup news. For Yelich fans, the news is especially important.
- LF: Jackson Chourio
- 1B: Vaughn
- C: Gary Sanchez
- SS: Cooper Pratt
- RF: Luis Lara
- 2B: David Hamilton
Starting Pitcher: Robert Gasser.
Judging from the roster for today's game, Gary Sanchez is coming in while Yelich comes out. William Contreras moves to designated hitter to make room for Sanchez.
Yelich is a 34-year-old slugger, while Sanchez is a 33-year-old catcher for the Brewers.
Looking At Christian Yelich & Gary Sanchez
Yelich is a 14-year MLB veteran who has been with the Brewers for nine seasons.
Over his career, he has been an All-Star several times, culminating in an NL MVP award in 2018. Yelich has enjoyed a solid 2026 campaign, notching 101 hits, 57 RBIs, 11 stolen bases, and 11 home runs in 112 games.
On the other hand, Sanchez has 44 hits, 35 RBIs, and 11 home runs in 83 games.
Pat Murphy on Christian Yelich
Recently, the Brewers manager has discussed Yelich's work ethic and his dedication to the game.
"I just remember he was here one night till 1 o'clock in the morning. A lot of guys in his situation, you've won MVP, you've been an all-star multiple times, you've done all the things in the game, you are 12 years in your career, and you know what: he still cares so much about the Milwaukee Brewers. That's the beauty of this whole thing…you have no idea how much this guy cares," Murphy said via a social media clip from Hunter Baumgardt.
